lines: Nigeria today. Five stories people are talking about, explained in about two minutes.
First, Ebola.
Nigeria's only confirmed case this year was a traveller from Uganda, confirmed in Abuja on October twentieth and later evacuated to Switzerland.
Two suspected cases in Adamawa tested negative after two rounds of testing.
The N.C.D.C. says there is no active case. Sixty-two contacts are being monitored, with the last expected to finish on November thirteenth.
If you have fever, bleeding or severe weakness after possible exposure, seek care, and call the N.C.D.C. on six-two-three-two.
Second, the voter register.
INEC says some registration officials abused their access to create fake records, including photos that appear to be A.I.-generated.
Its I.C.T. director says about one and a half million of the eleven million new registrations were flagged as suspicious.
The rights group SERAP wants an independent probe. INEC says the register will be cleaned up before it is certified on December fifteenth.
Third, the seventy-thousand-naira transport allowance.
The federal government agreed with the Nigeria Labour Congress to pay public servants seventy thousand naira a month for six months, starting this November.
But the Trade Union Congress rejected it, saying workers need a real pay rise, not a temporary allowance. Labour is now openly divided.
Fourth, borrowing.
The government has sent a five-year external borrowing plan of up to twenty-one point seven billion dollars to the National Assembly.
The finance minister says about ten point six billion is for transport, including coastal highways and railways, and that not all of it may be drawn.
And finally, some good news.
The Flamingos beat Venezuela one-nil with an eighty-ninth-minute penalty, to reach the semi-finals of the Under-Seventeen Women's World Cup.
They face Brazil on Wednesday, November fourth, in Rabat, chasing their first ever final.
That's Nigeria today. Check facts with official sources before you share.
